title: Session cache: Redis vs Memcached
brief: Logins store a session in a cache in front of a session store sized for cache misses only. 50k requests/s, 95% reads. Side A uses Redis with AOF persistence and a replica per node; side B uses Memcached, which has neither. Run each scenario and decide which you would pick, and when.

scenarios.label: Restart the cache
scenarios.about: At 10 s the whole cache restarts (down for 2 s). Redis reloads its keys from the AOF file; Memcached comes back empty.
scenarios.watch: At 10 s both caches go down for 2 s. Watch the hit ratio on each cache block and the store behind it: Memcached comes back empty, so its store takes every read and turns red until the cache warms up.

scenarios.label: Lose 1 of 3 nodes
scenarios.about: At 10 s a cache node dies and isn't replaced (3 nodes become 2). Watch the hit ratio and the session store.
scenarios.watch: At 10 s each cache drops from 3 nodes to 2. Watch the hit ratio: Memcached loses the keys that lived on that node, so more reads fall through and p99 rises.

scenarios.label: Steady 50k rps
scenarios.about: Nothing fails. What does Redis's durability cost when nothing goes wrong?
scenarios.watch: Nothing breaks, so both canvases look the same. Read the cost row in the table.

questions: What does Redis's replica and persistence cost per hour, and what does it buy?
If losing sessions only means users log in again, is Memcached good enough?
Which side would you size the session store differently for, and how?
The sim doesn't model data structures or multi-key operations. When would those decide it for Redis?
hints: Where do requests go when the cache doesn't have the key?
Compare the lowest cache hit row with the session store's load in each scenario. The session store is sized for 10% misses.

Redis pays about double per node for replicas. That buys a flat hit ratio when nodes die or restart. Memcached is cheaper and fine if the store behind it can take a cold cache, or if losing sessions is acceptable.
_notes: Graph: client -> api (20 x 10k) -> cache (3 nodes, hit 0.9, write-through) -> sessions kv (2 x 10k = 20k). Normal misses: 47.5k reads x 10% + 2.5k writes = 7.25k (rho 0.36). Redis: 3 x 2 x $0.219 (replica doubles), Memcached 3 x $0.219: sim cost $3.91 vs $3.26/hr. Lose a node (3 -> 2, replication none): Memcached keeps 2/3 of keys, hit 60%, misses 21.5k > 20k: sim p99 ~490 ms, recovers in ~8 s as it warms (30 s warm-up constant, estimate). Redis fails over to the replica: flat. Restart (down 10-12 s): both fail during the 2 s; Redis keeps its keys (AOF), recovers in ~2 s, errors 2.2%; Memcached starts cold, the session store gets the full 50k (rho 2.5), retries pile on: errors 14.3%, recovery ~52 s. Memory cost per GB of data (cache.r7g.large, 13.07 GiB): Redis with replica $0.034, Memcached $0.017/GB-hr. Not modeled: data structures, multi-key ops. Checked in frontend/src/lessons/content.test.ts. Real-world source: 'Scaling Memcache at Facebook' (NSDI 2013): look-aside cache, filled on demand; a write deletes the cached key instead of updating it (deletes are idempotent); leases stop thundering herds after a miss; when a node fails, a small Gutter pool (about 1% of servers) takes over its keys instead of rehashing them onto the remaining nodes, which cut client-visible failures by 99%. Worth raising when the lesson kills a cache node.
